# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical reading: Varga & Holm, comment on the Halden pilot

Sections 1–5 are a valuable re-analysis. The attrition finding is new and important, and the output and hours corrections confirm problems that could only be suspected from the working paper. The conclusion is the problem. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the comment's own residual estimate and by the Varden trial it cites. The comment also contains several internal inconsistencies.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Table 2, row 2 | 95.1 / 0.8 = 118.9 | ✓ |
| Table 2, row 3 | 98.4 / 0.859 = 114.6 | ✓ |
| Table 2, row 4 | 95.4 / 0.861 = 110.8 | ✓ |
| Hours, 27 orgs | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%) | ✓ |
| Hours, 17 orgs | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%) | ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 (−2.6%) | ✓ |
| Hours decomposition | 4 days × +0.7 h + 1.6 h on day off = 4.4 h above 32, about 36.4 h/week | ✗ Reported 34.6 |
| Novelty extrapolation | Energy falls 0.32 SD over 3 months; 0.29 SD left gives baseline at about month 8.7 | ✗ Reported "around month ten" |
| Attrition reasons | 6 + 2 = 8 of 9 | One withdrawal unaccounted for |

The hours decomposition matters most. The components don't add up to the reported total, by about 2 hours a week. Either the "+0.7 hours per day" figure is wrong, or it is measured against a different baseline, such as actual baseline days of about 8.06 hours rather than scheduled 8-hour days. Even on that reading the total is about 35.8 hours, so it still doesn't reconcile. The 34.6 figure feeds Table 2, so this needs explaining.

## 1. Attrition: the strongest finding, but it is not actually corrected

The microdata show that 7 of the 9 withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule started, mostly citing workload. This directly contradicts the working paper's "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." It is a significant misreport by the original authors and the comment's most important contribution.

It also affects a figure the comment doesn't revisit:
- Of the 68 organisations that actually began the schedule, 56 continued (82%), not 92%.
- Of all 70 enrolled, 80% continued.

However:
- **The abstract says** "correcting the first three" problems, which include attrition. **Table 2 corrects** only the output and hours problems. All four rows are survivor samples.
- **No bound is given.** The microdata include some months of data for the 7 organisations that started and then left. The comment could have computed bounds for those 7 or run a simple worst-case imputation for them, but neither is reported.

The attrition bias is argued well. It just isn't quantified.

## 2. Output measure: the gap is real, but some records may be the wrong measure

The gap is convincing: 19 of 23 organisations show manager-reported output above record-based output, which gives a two-sided sign-test p ≈ 0.003.

Two qualifications apply:
- **"Billable hours delivered" is partly an input measure.** It falls mechanically when hours fall. Using it as "output" biases the record-based index downward in exactly the setting being tested. The comment should show the comparison with and without hours-based records.
- **The records may be narrower than what managers rated.** Records such as tickets closed or units produced may miss quality and non-countable work that managers were weighing. This doesn't excuse the systematic upward rounding, but it means the 3.8-point gap is not all bias.

## 3. Table 2 compares different samples

The fall from +23.4% to +10.8% mixes two things:
1. the corrections themselves;
2. a change in sample from 61 organisations to 17.

The data note concedes this, but the abstract and conclusion present the fall as the effect of correction.

The clean test is simple: report all four specifications on the same 17 organisations. If the manager-reported, scheduled-hours estimate for those 17 is itself well below 23.4%, part of the "correction" is really composition.

The 17 organisations with both records and time tracking are probably more measurement-oriented, and plausibly more in software and professional services. They are not a neutral subset.

## 4. Revenue: right direction, crude deflator

Pointing out that the +1.4% is nominal is correct. I made the same point about the original. But:
- CPI is a consumer-price index, not the output-price index for these organisations' sectors.
- There is still no comparison group. Real revenue for comparable non-participating firms over the same period may also have fallen.

So −2.6% real is as uninterpretable as +1.4% nominal, just in the other direction.

## 5. Sectoral claims: the reasoning is right, but one threshold needs updating

The comment correctly says that with hours cut by 20%, any output index above 80 shows as a per-hour gain. By its own corrected hours (ratio 0.86), the break-even is about 86, not 80.

The retail figure from records (−11.2%) rests on only 3 organisations. Calling the Varden counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature" is defensible, but it rests on 5 v 5 offices.

## 6. Novelty: plausible, but argued from the wrong data

Several problems weaken this section:

- **Two points don't make a trend.** Linear extrapolation from two survey points can't distinguish decay to zero from a plateau. A plateau is a common pattern after an initial bump. As noted above, the extrapolation is also computed wrongly.
- **Energy is not output.** The comment infers decay in productivity from decay in self-reported energy.
- **The better test was available.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*, and the comment has the microdata. A month-by-month output trend is the direct test of novelty decay, and it isn't reported.
- **"Staff chose" is inaccurate.** At Halden, *organisations* volunteered and all staff in participating units moved. In Varden, offices were randomised and staff did not choose at all, yet per-hour gains still appeared over nine months.
- **"The burden of proof" works in both directions.** Failing to rule out novelty does not establish that the effect is novelty. It justifies the comment's (sensible) call for 18+ month follow-up, not the conclusion that the gain is an artifact.

## 7. The meetings critique is factually off and conceptually confused

**The facts.** Varden collected meeting data in *month six* at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. The comment says the analysis was "selected for analysis after the results were known." That is not what the trial reports. Varden's authors also:
- labelled the analysis exploratory;
- noted the seven-office limitation themselves;
- registered a confirmatory test.

They did not present it as an established mechanism. The scepticism about r = 0.71 across seven offices is warranted; the 95% CI is roughly −0.1 to 0.95. But the comment is attacking a stronger claim than Varden made.

**The concept.** The meetings hypothesis is not an artifact explanation. If cutting low-value meetings raises output per hour worked, that is a real productivity gain. It just might be achievable *without* cutting hours. That is a challenge to the policy's necessity, not to the reality of the gain. Dismissing it sits awkwardly with the claim that gains are "entirely an artifact."

## 8. The conclusion contradicts the evidence the comment relies on

"Entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" does not follow from the comment's own analysis:

- **Its own best estimate is a gain.** After its corrections, a +10.8% gain remains. Attributing all of it to novelty rests on the weak argument in §6.
- **It cites Varden selectively.** It uses Varden's counter stratum and ignores the case-processing stratum. That stratum shows +12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4) with:
  - randomisation, so no selection;
  - administrative output, so no manager inflation;
  - timesheet hours, so no scheduled-hours denominator.

  Of the comment's three artifacts, only novelty could still apply, and Varden staff did not choose the change.
- **It overgeneralises.** It moves from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

## Bottom line

**What the comment establishes:**
- The Halden working paper misreported its attrition.
- Manager-rated output ran about 4 points above organisations' own records.
- Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.
- Revenue fell in real terms.
- The Halden headline of +23.4% is substantially overstated.

**What it does not establish:**
- that per-hour gains are zero. Both its own residual (+10.8%) and the randomised Varden case-processing result (+12.5%) point to a real but modest gain in work that isn't tied to presence.
- that the gain is novelty. This remains an open question that the Halden monthly data could have addressed and longer follow-up will settle.

A defensible conclusion would be: *"Corrected for measurement, per-hour gains are roughly half those reported, concentrated in non-coverage work, and of unknown durability."* That is a strong and useful critique. "Entirely an artifact" overreaches in the same way the original "sector-general" claim did.

**Before publication, the comment should:**
- reconcile the hours decomposition;
- report the Table 2 specifications on a common sample;
- bound the attrition effect using the withdrawn organisations' partial data;
- examine the monthly output trend;
- correct its description of the Varden meetings analysis.
